Putting a lot of work into my car (about to get it painted and planning on some later performance upgrades) so I want to make sure I preserve the car and protect against any salt/whatever is used on the roads in the winter.

I'm from south central Texas so this is my first time dealing with snow/ice, and I don't really know what to expect.

Is there a good way to keep my car clean and protected for the winter months in Kansas, or should I invest in a winter beater? I know winters can vary in intensity and roughness towards cars depending on how the cities handle the roads, not sure how bad Kansas is.

You already answered your own question. Any vehicle you want to keep corrosion free long term really should not be driven on salted roads in the winter.

If a winter beater isn't an option I would suggest weekly washings with focus on wheel wells and the undercarriage. Even if you can't get the major body panels every week, atleast hit the underside and get all the crevices.

Some vehicles are just poorly designed with problem areas susceptible to corrosion. That being said, any factory holes on the frame and body that DONT have drainage holes, I would put a piece of good duct tape over it like Gorilla tape or even buy some rubber plugs of various shapes and sizes at the auto parts store and plug them up to prevent salt, sand etc from accumulating in pockets. Any seams or holes that do have drainage flush those out as often as possible and keep the drains clear so they can drain and air dry.

For a protection type chemical, there are numerous and you can search to your hearts content on the merits of each kind. Everyone has an opinion on what they thing works best but, I use a product called LPS 3 which is a waxy type film that never really dries, stays a little tacky. It's sold in aerosol, spray and gallon jugs. It's fluid enough to flow into areas when first sprayed but then sets up a bit to build a nice protective layer. Safe on paint, and you can just go nuts on everything underneath, rocker panels, frame, axles etc. Lots of folks recommend Fluid Film, another popular product or Boeshield, Waxoyl. I did some searching and there were some comparison tests done with some of those and the LPS 3 seemed to offer the longest lasting protection.

Mostly, keep it clean, let it dry regularly, identify problem areas and keep after them but it's always an uphill battle. The steps I mentioned above have worked pretty well for me.

Fantastic write up man, thank you very much.

A winter beater is likely out of the question for this year, but I should be able to afford a second car for 2017 winter. I'll just have to religiously follow your advice for upkeep and keep the car maintained this year around.

Thanks guys!

Drive it until before you expect the first snow. Give yourself enough time to do your usual storage prep, and leave it until after the risk of snow/ice events is pasted, and the spring rains have thoroughly washed the roads down. Yes, invest in a winter beater.
